clips.text: You come down from a hundred and seventy metres — and the ground does not forgive you.
One jump. A hundred and seventy metres into the sky — nearly twice the Statue of Liberty. The jump is not the story. The landing is.
Next: the spring, the launch, the flight — and the landing, explained. Rewind with me.
This is the morning after. You lie in the grass, legs folded wrong, the meadow towering over you like a forest. You jumped like a flea. You landed like a human.
Minutes ago you stood here, on this same grass, looking up at a single blade taller than you are. A flea could clear it in one bound. You wanted to know what that felt like.

Here is the problem, plainly. A flea weighs less than a milligram — about seven-tenths of one, in the fleas Cambridge filmed. You weigh about seventy kilograms. One hundred million times heavier. Same legs, same jump — a very different landing.
Because the jump was never the hard part. The hard part is coming down. To understand why, we rewind — to a spring inside a chest smaller than a grain of rice.
Chapter two: the spring. Forget muscles. Your legs could never do this alone — no muscle on Earth fires fast enough. The flea cheats. It stores the jump first, then lets it go.

First: the squeeze. Two great muscles in the flea's chest contract slowly, pressing on a pad of resilin — a rubbery protein, springier than any rubber we make. The energy waits in the pad, like a drawn bow.

Resilin gives back almost everything it takes. Stretch it to more than three times its length, let go, and it returns up to ninety-seven percent of the energy — only three percent lost as heat. A rubber band wishes it were resilin.

Second: the latch. The legs lock while the muscles keep squeezing. Nothing moves. The spring is loaded, the catch is holding, and the flea is, for a long moment, a loaded catapult pretending to be an insect.
Third: the release. A small muscle shifts the catch, the latch slips, and all that stored energy fires at once. No muscle could move this fast. The spring does the jumping; the muscle only loads it.

Here is what it is not: trying harder. You cannot jump like a flea by training your legs. Muscle fires in hundredths of a second; this launch takes about one-thousandth. The difference is not strength. It is a spring.
So the spring is loaded, the latch is set — and the whole jump is about to happen in less time than a blink. That is the launch.
Chapter three: the launch. In 2011, Sutton and Burrows filmed hedgehog fleas with high-speed cameras at Cambridge — and settled a mystery that had stood since 1967.

The push lasts about one point four milliseconds. One point four thousandths of a second. Your fastest blink takes a hundred times longer. In that sliver of time, the flea goes from still to nearly two metres a second.

And the force? The flea takes off at more than a hundred times the pull of gravity — the filmed jumps peaked near a hundred and fifty. A roller coaster pulls about four. You, jumping, manage two or three.

Slow that launch down and something strange appears. The flea does not push with its knees. It pushes through its feet — the tips of its shin bones, down onto its toes. The knee leaves the ground early; the foot does the work.

For forty-four years, scientists argued about which part of the leg did the pushing. The films ended it: the force runs from the spring in the chest, through the leg like a lever, down to the toes. Feet, not knees.

Now the cousin that does it even harder. The meadow froghopper — a six-millimetre bug on a grass stem — launches at more than four hundred times gravity. Its best jumps hit four hundred and eight. The flea is fast. The froghopper is a cannon.
The froghopper's trick is a bow, not a pad: a curved arch of hard cuticle and resilin, bent like an archery bow, then released. Different spring, same idea — store it slow, spend it all at once.
So the launch is a catapult, not a muscle. And a catapult, once fired, cannot steer. Which is fine — until you remember how high you are going. That is the flight.

Chapter four: the flight. Take the flea's jump — roughly a hundred times its body length — and give it to a human a hundred and seventy centimetres tall. The arithmetic says a hundred and seventy metres. Straight up.

Picture it. The Statue of Liberty stands ninety-three metres from the ground to the torch. Your jump clears her — and keeps rising, to nearly twice her height. One bound, and you are looking down at the torch.
Or count it in floors. A hundred and seventy metres is about fifty storeys. You leave the pavement, pass the fiftieth floor, and only then — at the top of the arc — do you stop rising.

How fast are you moving at takeoff? To climb a hundred and seventy metres, you must leave the ground at about fifty-eight metres a second — over two hundred kilometres an hour. Faster than a car on a motorway. Straight up.

And here is the honest boundary. That hundred and seventy metres is arithmetic, not an experiment. Nobody has built a human flea. The flea's best jumps — forty-eight centimetres across, seventeen up — are measured records, not every jump. The hundred-times figure is rough, not a constant.
But the arithmetic is the point. Scale the spring up, and the height follows — the same way scaling the flea's weight up changes everything about the fall. Which brings us back to the grass.
In the air, you are weightless for a few seconds — the longest fall of your life, stretched above a meadow. Below you, grass blades stand like trees. The ground waits, patient as ever.
A flea spends its whole life doing this — leaping, landing, leaping again, a hundred times its own height, without a thought. To the flea, the air is a highway. To you, it is a countdown.

So you are up there, two hundred kilometres an hour at takeoff, fifty storeys high — and gravity has already started collecting. What comes down is the part the flea never worries about. That is the landing.

Chapter five: the landing. Why does the flea walk away from falls that would kill you? The answer is the square-cube law — the rule that says when you grow, your weight grows faster than your strength.

Make an animal ten times bigger, and its weight grows a thousand times — while its legs grow a hundred times thicker. Strength cannot keep up with weight. The flea is small enough that the maths forgives it. You are not.

A flea falling from any height is slowed by the air itself. Its body is so light, and its surface so large for its weight, that air drag catches it like a parachute. It drifts down. You fall like a stone.

Now your landing. You come down at the speed you left — about fifty-eight metres a second, two hundred kilometres an hour. Your legs, built for a walking animal, must stop a hundred million times the flea's weight in a fraction of a second. They cannot. That is the twist: the jump is the easy part.
So here is the question the story turns on: if you could jump a hundred times your height — but every landing would break you — would you still take the jump?
There is no right answer. Only the answer your legs give — written the first time you looked down from fifty storeys. Which brings us to today. That is the choice.
One last thing: thank a flea the size of a grain of rice, a froghopper on a grass stem, and three teams who measured the impossible — then thank the air for being so gentle with small things.

Chapter six: today. You still stand in the meadow, still look up at a grass blade taller than you are, still feel the jump you will never take. Nothing has changed — except you know what that jump would cost.

Remember the numbers: about one point four milliseconds to launch; more than a hundred times gravity at takeoff; roughly a hundred times body length; a hundred and seventy metres for a human. One spring, and physics in your way.

And remember the twist: the enemy was never the height. It was the landing. The flea's spring is a gift only the small can afford — the jump is free, the landing is the price. The flea pays in milligrams. You pay in bones.
If you could jump 100 times your height but the landing would break you — where would you jump first? Tell us why.

Science note, plainly: forty-eight centimetres and seventeen are best-measured records, not every jump; a hundred times is a rough scale factor, not a constant; a hundred and seventy metres is scaling arithmetic, not an experiment; and recent work suggests resilin alone may store only a small share of the flea's jump energy — the spring is real; the rest is still being measured.

The named sources, so you can check me: Cadiergues, Joubert and Franc's flea jumps, 2000, in Veterinary Parasitology; Sutton and Burrows' flea mechanics, 2011, in the Journal of Experimental Biology; Bennet-Clark and Lucey's resilin spring, 1967; and Burrows' froghopper jumps, 2003 and 2006.
You come down from a hundred and seventy metres — and the ground does not forgive you. Next time you see a flea vanish from a dog's back, you will know: it did not fly. It fired a spring.
The jump was never the miracle. The landing was always the price. Goodnight. And if you ever wish you could jump like a flea — remember, the flea never has to land like you.
